title: Flag of Germany
wiki_lead:
The national flag of Germany is a tricolour consisting of three equal horizontal bands displaying the national colours of Germany: black, red, and gold (German: Schwarz-Rot-Gold). The flag was first sighted in 1848 in the German Confederation. The flag was also used by the German Empire from 1848 to 1849. It was officially adopted as the national flag of the German Reich (during the period of the Weimar Republic) from 1919 to 1933, and has been in use since its reintroduction in the Federal Republic of Germany in 1949.
Since the mid-19th century, Germany has had two competing traditions of national colours, black-red-gold and black-white-red. Black-red-gold were the colours of the 1848–1849 Revolutions, the Weimar Republic of 1919–1933 and the Federal Republic (since 1949). They were also adopted by the German Democratic Republic (1949–1990).
The colours black-white-red appeared for the first time in 1867 in the constitution of the North German Confederation. This nation state of Prussia and other north and central German States was expanded to the south German states in 1870–71, under the name German Empire. It kept these colours until the revolution of 1918–19. Thereafter, black-white-red became a symbol of the political right. The Nazis (National Socialist German Workers' Party) re-established these colours along with the party's own swastika flag in 1933. After World War II, black-white-red was still used by some conservative groups or by groups of the far right, as it is not forbidden, unlike specific Nazi symbols such as the aforementioned swastika.
Black-red-gold is the official flag of the Federal Republic of Germany. As an official symbol of the constitutional order, it is protected against defamation. According to §90a of the German penal code, the consequences are a fine or imprisonment up to three years.

Origins
The German association with the colours black, red, and gold surfaced in the radical 1840s, when the black-red-gold flag was used to symbolise the movement against the Conservative Order, which was established in Europe after Napoleon's defeat.
There are many theories in circulation regarding the origins of the colour scheme used in the 1848 flag. It has been proposed that the colours were those of the Jena Students' League (Jenaer Burschenschaft), one of the radically minded Burschenschaften banned by Metternich in the Carlsbad Decrees. The colours are mentioned in their canonical order in the seventh verse of August Daniel von Binzer's student song Zur Auflösung der Jenaer Burschenschaft ("On the Dissolution of the Jena Students' League") quoted by Johannes Brahms in his Academic Festival Overture. Another claim goes back to the uniforms (mainly black with red facings and gold buttons) of the Lützow Free Corps, which were mostly worn by university students and were formed during the struggle against the occupying forces of Napoleon. grok_lead: The national flag of Germany, known in German as Schwarz-Rot-Gold, is a horizontal tricolour featuring three equal stripes of black at the top, red in the middle, and gold at the bottom. Article 22(2) of the Basic Law for the Federal Republic of Germany designates these coloursâblack, red, and goldâas the federal flag, which was officially adopted on 23 May 1949 following the promulgation of the Basic Law. The black-red-gold design traces its origins to the liberal-nationalist movements of the early 19th century, particularly the Burschenschaften student fraternities and the flags flown during the March Revolution of 1848, where it symbolized demands for constitutional governance, unity among German states, and civic freedoms against monarchical absolutism. This tricolour served as the provisional flag of the Frankfurt Parliament in 1848â1849 and was later reinstated as the national flag of the Weimar Republic from 1919 to 1933. Under the Nazi regime (1933â1945), the black-red-gold was suppressed in favour of the black-white-red imperial colours and the swastika-emblazoned flag, associating the tricolour with opposition to authoritarianism. Following Germany's division after World War II, the Federal Republic ( West Germany) restored the black-red-gold as its flag in 1949 to emphasize democratic continuity and rupture from Nazi symbolism, while the German Democratic Republic ( East Germany) initially adopted a similar design but added the state coat of arms in 1959. Upon reunification on 3 October 1990, the plain black-red-gold tricolour became the exclusive national flag of the unified Federal Republic of Germany. The flag 's proportions are officially 3:2, though variants exist for state use (incorporating the federal eagle) and maritime ensigns. Today, it represents national identity, with its colours evoking historical aspirations for a free and united Germany, flown on public buildings and during official events as mandated by federal protocol.
